collectionunit.notes: “Most coring was carried out with a D section corer but a Livingstone corer and a piston corer utilising a tripod and winch were employed in stiff basal sediments at Kosipe A (KPA) and Neon Basin sites. Selected cores from five sites were described in the field and then wrapped and returned to the Australian National University (ANU) in Canberra. In the laboratory 8–15 cm sections of peat were sieved and the fine fraction (<200 mm) submitted for radiocarbon dates to the Sydney, Geochron and ANU laboratories. To clarify the stratigraphy of KPA and KPC, further dates were extracted from 1 to 2 cm core sections. The fine fraction was pre-treated with acid–alkali–acid before submission to ANSTO for AMS dating. Other samples were collected at 20 cm intervals and analysed for pollen and microcharcoal using standard preparation methods.”-(Hope, 2009)

site.sitedescription: “The dryland vegetation at Kosipe is a mixed montane forest with a diverse canopy that includes Castanopsis acumanitissima, Galbulimima belgraveana, Fagrea salticola, scattered Nothofagus grandis, Ficus spp., Podocarpus, Phyllocladus hypophyllus, Dacrycarpus Araucaria cunninghamii, Elaeocarpus spp., Syzygium effusum, Planchonella, Cryptocarya, Litsea, Weinmannia and Schizomeria. Understory trees include Ilex, Homolanthus, Macaranga and Schefflera. The river corridor and some ridge crests have been cleared for gardens and are in a stage of regrowth of tall grasses such as Sacharum and secondary shrubs such as Acalypha, Saurauia and Eurya. A prominent tree of clearings is P. julianetti, a large pandan to 20 m whose fruits are an important seasonal staple for the area. Wetland vegetation consists of a low swamp forest dominated by Dacrydium nidulum but with numerous other species including Castanopsis, Xanthomyrtus, Sericolea, Podocarpus, Vaccinium and Dimorphanthera with scattered Cyathea tree ferns. A small aquatic Pandanus is common as an understory shrub and Freycinetia is a common climber. The forest grows where some silts are present in the upper layers of the peat. On deep peats the sites are dominated by sedges including Scirpus sp which forms a tall sedgeland up to 2 m in height in the centre of the swamp and Eleocharis sphacelata along stream lines. Melastoma and Gonocarpus are low shrubs and ferns like Blechnum and Gleichenia and fern allies such as Lycopodium spp. are common. Sedgelands of Saceiolepis indica together with scattered grasses such as Pennisetum occur in more disturbed places with herbs including Ranunculus, Gentiana and Eriocaulon. Below Kosipe the forests are more mixed and have an increasing lowland component such as palm species. But these have not been investigated closely although they were extensively collected by the First Archbold Expedition in 1933 (Archbold and Rand, 1935). Above 2200 m the forest loses many taxa such as Castanopsis–Lithocarpus and Calophyllum and the proportion of conifers increases together with Xanthomyrtus, Rapanea, Polyosma and Ericaceae. Nothofagus forms gregarious patches up to 2500 m but is nowhere extensive.”-(Hope, 2009)
